description: I’m an independent student researcher with interests in healthcare innovation, AI-driven solutions, and data-informed problem-solving. Through projects involving assistive technology and intelligent health systems, I’ve explored how technology can address real-world challenges.
summary: AETHER (Astronaut Health Evaluation, Tracking & Early Response) is an offline-capable astronaut health intelligence prototype designed to support crew health monitoring during long-duration space missions. It brings together simulated or manually entered crew health indicators, cabin-environment readings, mission context, and NASA space-weather information in one interface. AETHER analyzes trends against a synthetic demonstration baseline, identifies concurrent changes across multiple indicators, and presents explainable, confidence-labeled insights to help users recognize patterns that may warrant attention. It also includes measurement guidance, mission routines, a reference knowledge base, and local data management. When online, it retrieves public space-weather context from NASA DONKI and research and media resources from NASA services. When offline, its cached application shell and locally stored information support continued access to core features. AETHER is an experimental decision-support prototype, not a medical device; its demo data are synthetic and its outputs require review by qualified flight medical personnel.
details:
How it works and what it provides

AETHER organizes mission health information into connected modules: Mission Overview, Crew Health, Space Environment, Health Intelligence, AETHER Assistant, NASA Updates, Measurement Guide, Body & Hazards, Mission Routine, and Medical Operations.

Crew indicators include resting heart rate, blood pressure, sleep, temperature, mood/readiness, glucose, and exercise. Environmental indicators include cabin CO₂, radiation context, temperature, and humidity. Demo readings are generated synthetic data, while users can enter their own readings manually.

The prototype compares readings with a synthetic baseline and generic reference ranges, identifies deviations and concurrent trends, and presents insights with confidence labels and evidence links. It does not diagnose conditions or determine medical readiness.

NASA resources and data

AETHER retrieves public solar-flare and solar energetic particle event information from NASA's DONKI API when online. It also references NASA Human Research Program material on spaceflight hazards and risks, searches NASA Technical Reports Server for research, and accesses NASA Image and Video Library search results. DONKI is used only as space-weather context; it is not treated as an onboard radiation dosimeter or a direct measurement of crew exposure.

Technology and design

The application is built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using browser storage for local entries and a service worker for caching the application shell and selected resources. It is designed to remain accessible when connectivity is limited, while clearly distinguishing cached information from live NASA data. The interface includes crew and medical views, trend visualizations, guided routines, exports, and privacy controls.

Innovation, impact, and limitations

AETHER brings health trends, environmental context, evidence references, and mission routines into one offline-capable interface. Its intended impact is to help crews and medical teams review patterns and organize information during missions where communication may be delayed or unavailable. It is an early-stage prototype: it has not been clinically validated, tested with astronauts, or approved by NASA. Crew and cabin demonstration readings are synthetic or manually entered, and all medical decisions remain with qualified flight medical personnel.
